content.audience_tension: The target audience — urban professionals aged 25-40 who make coffee at home and say they value ritual over convenience — live inside schedules built for speed. For most of that group, coffee on a weekday is something you get (a pod, a drip machine on autopilot, a coffee-shop stop) rather than something you make. The tension is between wanting mornings to feel intentional and self-directed, and defaulting to whatever costs the least time, because deliberately slowing down can feel indulgent or impractical on a Tuesday. The brief names this tension directly by setting 'ritual' against 'convenience' as competing values, by pricing the product at $38 (a considered purchase, not an impulse one), and by warning against generic luxury imagery — the tension is not 'I want to look rich,' it's 'I want five minutes that are mine before the day takes them.'
content.desired_behavior: A viewer sees the :15 vertical video or one of the two 4:5 stills on social, recognizes the five-minute pour-over moment as a version of a morning ritual they want for themselves (not as an ad for 'a kitchen gadget'), and takes a direct-response action: clicks through to the Solace DTC site and adds the $38 pour-over dripper to cart. The objective is explicitly DTC visits and add-to-carts, not brand-awareness alone, so the creative must carry a clear, low-friction path from feeling to action.
content.product_relevance: The ceramic pour-over cannot be a backdrop prop for a generic 'calm morning' mood — it has to be the literal mechanism that makes the ritual happen: the user stands at it, pours, waits, watches the water bloom the grounds. Its three verified attributes reinforce that role rather than sit apart from it: hand-glazed stoneware and small-batch production make the object itself read as considered and singular (supporting 'ritual', not 'appliance'), while dishwasher-safe care keeps the ritual repeatable on an ordinary Tuesday rather than precious or occasional. This is how the strategy satisfies the brief's required 'clear product role in the story' and 'readable closing product moment' without leaning on unverified performance claims (e.g., taste, extraction quality, temperature control) that were not supplied as facts.
content.single_minded_proposition: The Solace pour-over is the five hands-on minutes you take back for yourself before the day takes the rest of your time — a small, repeatable act of choosing slow on purpose. (This operationalizes the brief's own key message, 'A five-minute ritual that slows your morning down, on purpose,' as a proposition the creative director can build routes against.)
proof_points: Hand-glazed stoneware ceramic (verified fact): each piece carries visible handmade variation, giving the object a tactile, one-of-a-kind quality that a mass-produced plastic or metal drip gadget cannot claim — supports 'ritual object' over 'kitchen appliance.'

Made in small batches (verified fact): reinforces a considered, non-commodity positioning consistent with a $38 price point and with the brief's instruction to avoid generic luxury imagery — the claim to make is 'made with care in limited runs,' not 'exclusive' or 'luxury.'

Dishwasher safe (verified fact): removes the plausible objection that a 'ritual' object is too precious or high-maintenance to use every weekday — the ritual survives real life, which is what makes it repeatable rather than a one-time novelty.

Structural (not brand-specific) pour-over mechanic: manual pour-over brewing requires the user's continuous attention for several minutes, unlike a pod or programmable drip machine — this is a general characteristic of the pour-over method and is treated here as a category fact, not a tested claim about the Solace product's performance, taste, or extraction quality.
success_criteria: Increase in click-throughs from the campaign's video and still placements to the Solace DTC product page, among the stated home-coffee-enthusiast audience segment.
Add-to-cart rate on site visits attributed to this campaign's creative, tracked against the campaign's own traffic (not an invented industry benchmark, since no baseline was supplied).

Qualitative signal that the 'ritual, on purpose' message is landing as intended — e.g., audience comments, saves, or shares that reference slowing down / morning ritual language rather than generic product-feature language.

Creative compliance checks the strategist can hand to the creative director and QC: every route keeps a clear, legible product role in the story and a readable closing product moment (both explicit brief requirements), and makes no performance, taste, or research claim beyond the three verified facts.

Note: no numeric targets (specific CTR%, add-to-cart %, conversion rate) are set here, because the brief and upstream context supplied no baseline or target figures; these should be defined by the producer/brand with actual analytics before being used as pass/fail thresholds.

hypotheses: Hypothesis: this audience associates fast-format coffee (pods, programmable drip machines, coffee-shop pickup) with the rushed pace of their weekday, creating an unmet desire for a deliberately slower alternative — this is a reasoned inference from the brief's own 'ritual over convenience' framing, not sourced audience or market research.

Hypothesis: for this audience, handmade/small-batch cues signal intentionality and self-care rather than status or luxury, which is why the proposition leans on 'ritual/self-possession' rather than premium framing — inferred from the brief's tone words and its explicit instruction to avoid generic luxury imagery, not from tested creative research.
Hypothesis: removing the 'high-maintenance object' concern (via dishwasher-safe care) meaningfully lowers a real adoption barrier to daily use — a plausible behavioral read, not a validated finding.

Hypothesis: a $38 price point sits in a 'considered but attainable' zone for this audience (enough to feel intentional, not so much it reads as a luxury purchase) — an inference from the price and audience description, not a tested pricing study.

routes.central_idea: Before the phone, the inbox, or anyone else gets a piece of you, there are five minutes that are only yours — marked by the pour.
routes.emotional_promise: Quiet self-possession: the felt relief of claiming a few minutes before the day starts claiming them for you.
routes.product_role: The Solace dripper is the literal boundary object. The film's one deliberate action — setting the phone face-down and reaching for the dripper instead — makes the product the mechanism of the choice, not a backdrop to it. It stays in frame through the pour, the bloom, and the final held mug, closing on an unhurried, fully lit shot of the dripper itself on the counter.
routes.visual_language: Quiet and continuous, no contrast-cutting: warm low window light, muted stoneware palette (terracotta, cream, soft grey), handheld-but-steady camera, close but not macro. Sound carries more of the emotion than music — water, steam, ceramic set down, a phone buzzing once, off-screen and ignored.
routes.execution_example: 15s / 9:16 (D01): Open tight on a phone screen lighting up on a counter; a hand turns it face-down without looking. Cut to the same hand lifting the Solace dripper, setting it on a mug, spooning grounds. Slow spiral pour, water blooming the grounds in close-up (2-3s held). Cut to the person at a window, mug in both hands, steam rising, a single distant notification sound goes unanswered. Final beat (2s): dripper alone on the counter in soft full light, product fully legible, with an illustrative closing line such as 'Made in small batches' (exact copy owned by copywriter). The two 4:5 stills (D02) pull directly from this beat structure: still 1 = the pour/bloom close-up with the dripper as clear hero object; still 2 = the closing counter shot, product fully visible and legible, doubling as a clean DTC-linkable product image.

routes.central_idea: The bloom itself — the moment water first meets the grounds — is the ritual's whole point, and the hand-glazed ceramic is filmed as the singular object that stages it.
routes.emotional_promise: Presence: the satisfaction of doing one small thing slowly enough to actually notice it happening.
routes.product_role: The dripper's surface and form are the visual subject, not just present in the shot. Macro texture on the hand-glazed stoneware (visible glaze variation, no two pieces identical) is used to make the tactile, handmade proof point legible on screen, then the frame pulls back to show the object in full use — giving the product both an intimate role and a clear closing moment.
routes.visual_language: Macro and shallow depth of field, slow motion on water contact and steam, warm directional morning light, near-silent sound design (pour, drip, a single ceramic clink) with minimal or no music. No other objects compete in frame — discipline here is what keeps it from reading as generic 'luxury lifestyle' imagery.
routes.execution_example: 15s / 9:16 (D01): Near-entirely macro — dry grounds catching light, first pour, the bloom rising and settling, steam curling off the surface, a fingertip resting briefly on the glaze's texture. In the last 3 seconds, camera pulls back for the first time to a clean, fully lit shot of the dripper and finished mug on the counter, with a hand entering frame to lift the mug — the human presence and the product both land together as the closing moment. Illustrative closing line: 'Hand-glazed. Small batch. Yours.' The two 4:5 stills (D02) isolate: still 1 = the bloom macro shot; still 2 = the pulled-back closing counter shot, framed as a clean product/DTC image.

routes.central_idea: An ordinary Tuesday, not a weekend — the deliberate choice to reach for the slow thing instead of the fast thing, on a day that gave no permission to slow down.
routes.emotional_promise: Quiet agency: permission to choose slowness even when nothing about the day is asking for it.
routes.product_role: The dripper is staged as the chosen alternative in an explicit two-beat decision (reach for the fast option, then don't — reach for this instead), which makes its role in the story unmissable. It remains the visual anchor through the pour and into a final in-focus product shot.
routes.visual_language: Two-beat structure with a movement contrast rather than a lighting contrast (to avoid a glossy before/after ad feel): a slightly quicker, handheld beat for the 'fast' cue, settling into a locked-off, steady frame for the pour. Same muted warm palette throughout so the shift feels like a change in pace, not a change in world.
routes.execution_example: 15s / 9:16 (D01): Opens on an out-of-focus stack of notifications/alarm on a phone, a hand starting to reach for it — then redirects to the Solace dripper sitting on the counter instead. One continuous, steady pour; the frame holds on the bloom. Final beat: person seated, mug in both hands, dripper still visible in soft foreground focus. On-screen line (illustrative, copywriter to finalize): 'A five-minute ritual, on purpose.' The two 4:5 stills (D02): still 1 = the redirected-hand moment (phone out of focus behind, dripper sharp in the foreground) carrying the tension itself; still 2 = the seated closing shot with the product legible in frame.

content.recommendation_rationale: R1 ("the line before the day") most directly dramatizes the strategy's own audience tension — ritual vs. the pull of convenience — through one specific, small, believable action (turning the phone face-down) rather than a generic mood board or an explicit before/after contrast edit. That keeps it furthest from the brief's 'generic luxury imagery without a story' risk while still giving the product an unambiguous role and a clean, legible closing shot that doubles easily as a DTC-linkable image. Its single continuous pace (no hard tonal cut) also fits the brief's 'quiet, warm, tactile' tone more precisely than R3's two-beat contrast, and it extends more naturally to both required still crops than R2's mostly-macro treatment, which risks losing legible product context if used as a static image on its own. R2 and R3 remain strong alternates: R2 is the more sensory, tactile-proof-point-forward option if the brand wants to foreground the hand-glazed/small-batch facts even more literally; R3 is the more literal, message-forward option if the producer wants the 'on purpose' contrast made explicit rather than implied.

assumptions: No real people are depicted or implied: any on-camera hands/figures in the execution examples are fictional, generic talent concepts, not a real individual's likeness — casting_director will formalize this in the casting_bible at the next stage.

No reference imagery was supplied with this brief (references: [] in the project record) and no reference_reader tool is bound in this run, so none was or could be visually inspected; the visual-language descriptions above are original creative direction, not derived from any inspected reference asset.

On-screen/closing lines quoted in the execution examples (e.g., 'Made in small batches', 'A five-minute ritual, on purpose') are illustrative placeholders to show how the required closing product moment could read; final wording is the copywriter's deliverable at the next stage, not locked copy.

Assumed the depicted moment is a solitary, at-home morning scenario (person alone, no household/family context), consistent with the brief's 'five-minute ritual... on purpose' framing and the strategist's audience read — this is a creative choice, not a stated brief requirement.
Assumed a single named location/setup (home kitchen counter, window light) is sufficient for a :15 spot and two stills; no additional location was specified in the brief.

Treated 'made in small batches' and 'hand-glazed' as visually demonstrable through texture/variation in-camera, and 'dishwasher safe' as better suited to supporting copy than to any on-screen visual, since it is not something a viewer can see in a shot.

story.logline: At 7:00 a notification lights NORA's phone. Her hand flips it face-down in passing and goes to the Solace dripper instead. When the day buzzes again, it gets as far as the rings in her coffee and no further until 7:05.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - 7:00 AM
beat_sheet.what_happens: Her phone lights up on the oak counter beside a chipped white mug: 7:00, and under it one notification banner too small to read. It buzzes. NORA's hand doesn't slow. It flips the phone face-down in passing, so the phone lands against the mug, and carries straight on right toward the dish rack out of frame. She lifts the Solace dripper out of the rack, and her thumb passes over the glaze pooled at its foot. We cut mid-carry, and the dripper seats on the mug with a click.
beat_sheet.turn: Someone wants her at 7:00 and she refuses them. The hand that refused goes to the dripper, and her five minutes start here.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - MOMENTS LATER
beat_sheet.what_happens: Cut to grounds already heaped in a pressed paper filter inside the dripper. NORA pours from out of frame. Only the gooseneck spout comes in from frame left, and a slow spiral lands on the grounds, which swell and dome up. Nothing else happens in frame.
beat_sheet.turn: The pour fills the time the flip started. The frame now belongs to the ritual, not the phone.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - MOMENTS LATER
beat_sheet.what_happens: A last drip falls as she lifts the dripper off the mug and sets it down just past it, so the phone, the mug and the dripper sit in a line. NORA's fingertips rest along the chipped mug's side below the rim, palm clear, with the heel of her hand on the oak counter. The phone rattles against the wood, and the coffee shivers into fine rings, with the dripper standing right there. The rattle stops, the rings flatten, and her hand stays where it is. Only then does the card come up: 'Everyone else gets you at 7:05.'
beat_sheet.turn: The day reaches into her cup and gets nothing. The dripper that drew the line is in frame. The card says when the day will get her: at 7:05.

beat_sheet.heading: INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER - MOMENTS LATER
beat_sheet.what_happens: The mug is gone. The Solace dripper stands empty on the counter, whole and legible, and the glaze mark her thumb crossed faces the lens. The phone is still face-down and dark at the edge of frame. 'Hand-glazed stoneware.' comes on screen, then the CTA, with a small 'Solace' sign-off beneath both.
beat_sheet.turn: She took the coffee and left the phone. The tool becomes the hero, and the viewer is told where to buy one.

deliverable_scripts.idea_in_one_line: At 7:00 the phone goes face-down and the dripper comes up. The next buzz reaches her coffee but not her, and nobody gets her until 7:05.

beats.picture: HOOK. A phone lies face-up on an oak counter with a chipped white mug right beside it. The lock screen lights: 7:00 in large readable digits, with one generic notification banner beneath it, its text too small to read. It buzzes. At about 0.8s NORA's hand comes in. The hand doesn't slow: it flips the phone in passing, the phone's edge lands against the mug, and the hand carries straight on right, toward the rack.
beats.sound: One phone buzz rattling on the counter, then the soft knock of the case landing on wood. Then silence.

beats.picture: Two angles. First angle: the same hand lifts the Solace dripper out of the dish rack. As the hand closes on it, the thumb passes over the glaze pooled unevenly at its foot without stopping, the mark B5 later turns to the lens. The hand sets off low and level. Cut mid-carry: the dripper comes in right to left and seats with a click on the chipped white mug, which still touches the face-down phone's edge. The hand lets go and stays clear of the phone. B2 ends on the empty dripper sitting on the mug. The card sits clear of the dripper in both angles.
beats.sound: A faint knock as the dripper leaves the dish rack; room tone across the cut; stoneware clicking onto the mug rim.
beats.on_screen_text: Nobody gets you before the pour.

beats.picture: Cut to grounds already heaped in a pressed paper filter inside the Solace dripper. A gooseneck spout comes in from frame left and pours a slow spiral onto them. The grounds swell, bubble and dome up against the paper. Hold on the bloom to the end of the beat.
beats.sound: A thin stream of water on wet grounds; the soft fizz of the bloom. No music.

beats.picture: NORA's hand lifts the Solace dripper off the chipped mug, and a last drip falls from its tip into the coffee. The hand sets the dripper down on the oak counter just past the mug, on the side away from the phone, so the three sit in a line: phone, mug, dripper. The coffee's surface is now open to the lens.
beats.sound: A last drip plinking into the coffee; stoneware set down on wood.

beats.picture: Phone, mug and dripper in a line on the oak counter. NORA's fingertips rest along the chipped mug's side below the rim, palm clear, the heel of her hand on the counter. The mug touches the face-down phone's edge. The Solace dripper stands just past the mug, on the side away from the phone, in frame for the whole beat. The phone rattles against the wood and the coffee shivers into fine rings. About 1.0s in, the rattle stops, the rings flatten, and her hand stays where it is. The card comes up at 9.5s as the rings flatten, holds to 11.5s, and sits clear of the dripper.
beats.sound: One phone buzz, about 1.0s long, rattling against the wood and ticking against the mug, left unanswered. It stops. Room tone.

beats.picture: Moments later the mug and hand are gone. The Solace dripper stands empty on the oak counter with its filter out. The glaze pooled unevenly at its foot, the mark her thumb crossed in B2, faces the lens. At the frame edge, clear of the dripper, the phone lies face-down and dark. The whole product is in frame and legible.
beats.sound: Room tone; off screen, the kettle ticking as it cools.

beats.picture: The B5 frame, held. The empty Solace dripper stands on the oak counter with the glaze pooled at its foot facing the lens, and the phone lies face-down and dark at the frame edge. The whole product is legible. Nothing in frame moves.
beats.sound: Room tone and the kettle ticking as it cools, to the last frame. No music, no sting.

deliverable_scripts.cta: Shop the Solace dripper. (Paid, primary: the platform's Shop Now button carries the DTC product-page link. Organic alternate card: 'Shop the Solace dripper. Link in bio.')

stills_copy.picture: The pour and the bloom. NORA's hand tips a gooseneck kettle, with its scorch band in frame, and a thin spiral of water lands on grounds domed up inside the Solace dripper. The dripper sits on a chipped white mug, and the mug touches the edge of a face-down phone. The copy stays clear of the dripper, the kettle and the pour.
stills_copy.headline: Nobody gets you before the pour.
stills_copy.subline: Hand-glazed stoneware, made in small batches. Shop the Solace dripper.

stills_copy.picture: The closing counter shot. The Solace dripper stands empty on a bare oak counter, with no filter, mug or phone. The glaze pooled unevenly at its foot faces the lens. The whole product is in frame and legible, and the copy sits clear of it. The textless plate doubles as the DTC product image.
stills_copy.headline: Out from 7:00. Back at 7:05.
stills_copy.subline: Hand-glazed, and it still goes in the dishwasher. Shop the Solace dripper.

decisions.choice: The hook is the phone flip. The lock screen shows 7:00 and one generic notification banner too small to read, and the phone buzzes once. NORA's hand doesn't slow: it flips the phone in passing and carries straight on toward the rack, all by 1.5s. There is no VO and no card over the hook.
decisions.reason: It is a specific action in the first frame, and it is R1's one deliberate choice. The banner makes the buzz a person wanting her rather than an alarm. With only the time on screen, a muted viewer would read the flip as a snooze. The readable 7:00 sets up the 7:05 card.
decisions.source: Craft brief: hook rule, 'observable action', sound-off rule; route R1 central idea: 'Before the phone, the inbox, or anyone else gets a piece of you'

decisions.choice: B1 stays on the phone and the mug. The hand leaves frame right toward the dish rack, and the rack is first seen in B2's first angle.
decisions.reason: B1 has to stay tight for 7:00 to read. The hand's exit is enough to show where the rack is.
decisions.source: Craft brief: sound-off rule

decisions.choice: B2 is two angles with a cut mid-carry: first the lift from the rack, then the dripper seating on the mug with a click. B2 ends on that click.
decisions.reason: Played whole, the carry can't run at habit pace in 3.0s. The cut keeps the two moments that show the product and drops the travel between them.
decisions.source: Brief tone: quiet; craft brief: 'Timing is a budget'

decisions.choice: In B2's lift, the thumb passes over the glaze pooled at the dripper's foot and doesn't stop. B5, B6 and D02-2 turn that same mark to the lens. No card or VO points at it.
decisions.reason: The fact is shown in use before it is named, so B5's 'Hand-glazed stoneware.' names something the viewer has already watched a hand touch. It adds the tactile note from the brief's tone, and a competitor's dripper can no longer be swapped in cleanly. Because the thumb doesn't stop, it reads as habit, not a caress for the camera.
decisions.source: Craft brief calibration: 'demonstrated rather than asserted'; brief tone: tactile; taste notes: 'The product is a tool, then a hero'; verified fact: hand-glazed stoneware

decisions.choice: The paper filter and grounds go in during the B2/B3 cut, so B3 opens on grounds already heaped in a pressed filter.
decisions.reason: This keeps the carry at habit pace, keeps her hand from reaching over the phone, and gives the product's first appearance time to land.
decisions.source: Brief key message: 'slows your morning down, on purpose'; tone: quiet

decisions.choice: Every card, the sign-off and all still copy sit in negative space, clear of the dripper in every angle.
decisions.reason: The product stays legible in every frame it appears in.
decisions.source: Craft brief: on-screen text never over the product

decisions.choice: In B3 only the gooseneck spout comes in, from frame left. The pouring hand and the kettle body stay out of frame. D02-1 carries the pouring hand and S2's real detail, the kettle's scorch band. For B3 this breaks 'One real detail per scene' on purpose.
decisions.reason: The bloom stays large, and it is the one held moment of the ritual. The detail isn't lost, because still 1 shows it at full size.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'One real detail per scene'; route R1 execution example: bloom held 2-3s

decisions.choice: New timings: B3 4.5-7.0 (the bloom holds 2.5s), B4a 7.0-8.5, B4b 8.5-11.5, B5 11.5-13.0, B6 13.0-15.0. In B4b the rattle and rings play for about 1.0s with no text. The 7:05 card comes up at 9.5s as the rings flatten and holds for 2.0s.
decisions.reason: The turn reads from the picture first, and the card then answers it instead of announcing it. The bloom stays inside the route's 2-3s hold. The product hold is 3.5s, above the 1.5s minimum.
decisions.source: Craft brief: sound-off rule, 'one card per roughly 2 seconds'; taste notes: 'Restraint over explanation'

decisions.choice: In B4a the dripper is set down just past the mug, so the phone, the mug and the dripper sit in a line. In B4b the dripper stands in frame on the side away from the phone while the phone rattles and the rings shiver and flatten.
decisions.reason: The picture now shows what the beat sheet claims. The buzz reaches the cup and stops at her hand, and the tool that drew the line is right there. The dripper stays in frame through the pour, the bloom and the held mug.
decisions.source: Route R1 product_role; brief must-include: 'A clear product role in the story'

decisions.choice: The second buzz reads through the coffee. The face-down phone rattles, and the coffee in the mug touching it shivers into fine rings. Then the rings flatten while NORA's fingertips stay put. The mug touches the phone from B1 on, because the flip lands the phone against it.
decisions.reason: With the sound off, the turn reads from something the camera can catch in any light. Lifting the dripper off in B4a uncovers the coffee, which gives the rings a surface to show on.
decisions.source: Craft brief: sound-off rule; quality bar: nothing physically implausible

decisions.choice: In B4b, NORA's fingertips rest along the chipped mug's side below the rim, with the palm clear and the heel of her hand on the oak counter.
decisions.reason: A full wrap would add mass and damp the vibration, which would mute the rings the turn depends on.
decisions.source: Quality bar: nothing physically implausible

decisions.choice: The coffee rings are the script's own real detail. The chipped mug and the dish rack stay as set texture, showing a dripper in daily use in a real kitchen.
decisions.reason: The rings are the one thing only this story would have.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'One real detail per scene'; brief must-avoid: generic luxury imagery

decisions.choice: I broke from the route's execution example on purpose and cut the window-and-mug shot. B4b replaces it with the second buzz, the rings and the hand that stays put.
decisions.reason: The window shot is the first thing the taste notes reject. The replacement keeps R1's idea and the product's role.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Anyone gazing out a window holding a mug'; route R1 product_role

decisions.choice: NORA appears only as hands and forearms. No face appears in the spot or in either still.
decisions.reason: Her hands carry the story. A face would pull the spot toward stock lifestyle footage.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Hands before faces'; craft brief: stock-lifestyle rejects

decisions.choice: The spot has no VO: 0 spoken words in 15s. The 7:00-to-7:05 idea lives in the lock screen and the two cards. The words 'five minutes' are never said or written on screen.
decisions.reason: As picture and cards, the idea reaches muted viewers, and the second buzz lands on its own in room tone.
decisions.source: Craft brief: timing budget and sound-off rule; taste notes: 'Restraint over explanation', 'Dry over sentimental'

decisions.choice: There is no music. Real sounds carry the mood: the buzz, the case knocking on wood, the dripper leaving the rack, stoneware clicking onto the mug rim, the pour, the bloom fizz, the last drip, stoneware set down on wood, the phone ticking against the mug and the kettle ticking as it cools.
decisions.reason: The taste notes allow music late, if at all. Without music, the second buzz stays audible, and that buzz is the turn.
decisions.source: Taste notes: 'Sound design before music'; route R1 visual_language

decisions.choice: B1's sound is 'the soft knock of the case landing on wood'.
decisions.reason: Face-down, the phone rests on the lip of its case, so the case touches the wood and the glass doesn't.
decisions.source: Quality bar: nothing physically implausible

decisions.choice: The product works as a tool from B2 to B4b and is the hero in B5-B6 for 3.5s. The mug is gone in B5-B6, and the phone stays face-down and dark at the frame edge. No coffee drips show on the outer glaze.
decisions.reason: The product is shown in use before it becomes the hero. She took the coffee and left the phone, so the last frames belong to this route. Drips on the DTC image would suggest a dripper that spills.
decisions.source: Brief must-include; craft brief: product moment; taste notes: 'The product is a tool, then a hero' and the ending reject

decisions.choice: The B5 card reads 'Hand-glazed stoneware.' from 11.5 to 13.0s. B6 holds the CTA from 13.0 to 15.0s.
decisions.reason: The fact is kept word for word and gets the same reading pace as the other cards. 'Made in small batches' appears on the D02-1 subline.
decisions.source: Brief must-include: 'A readable closing product moment'; taste notes: 'Restraint over explanation'

decisions.choice: A small 'Solace' sign-off line sits beneath both end cards from 11.5 to 15.0s and stays up across the B5/B6 change. It is written after '[sign-off]' in the B5 and B6 text. It never sits over the dripper or the phone's edge. It is type on the product frame, not a logo on a coloured card.
decisions.reason: A muted viewer can link the whole 3.5s product hold to the brand, and the product stays in frame the whole time.
decisions.source: Brief objective; must-include: 'A readable closing product moment'; taste notes: ending reject

decisions.choice: Paid is the primary cut. The B6 card reads 'Shop the Solace dripper.', and the platform's Shop Now button carries the DTC product-page link. Both still sublines end on 'Shop the Solace dripper.' The organic alternates stay word for word: B6 'Shop the Solace dripper. Link in bio.'; D02-1 'Hand-glazed stoneware, made in small batches. Shop the Solace dripper, link in bio.'; D02-2 'Hand-glazed, and it still goes in the dishwasher. Shop the Solace dripper, link in bio.'

decisions.choice: The D02-2 headline is now 'Out from 7:00. Back at 7:05.' I made the still hold both ends of the window on its own rather than tying it to carousel frame 2. D02-1 keeps 'Nobody gets you before the pour.'
decisions.reason: D02-2 is a bare plate with no phone, mug or clock, and the textless version is the DTC product image, so it will be served on its own. The line holds both clock times in 6 words. It has the dry edge of the out-of-office reply the audience writes every week, and it points straight at R1's 'the inbox'. Next to D02-1 it still reads as the film's before and after.
decisions.source: Brief key message; craft brief: sound-off rule (each asset reads from its own picture and text); taste notes: 'Dry over sentimental'; route R1 central idea

decisions.choice: Only the three verified facts are stated. Hand-glazed stoneware is shown by the thumb in B2 and stated on the B5 card and the D02-1 subline. 'Made in small batches' is on the D02-1 subline. Dishwasher safe appears only on D02-2, as 'it still goes in the dishwasher'. Nothing is said about taste, speed or quality, and the price stays off screen.

assumptions: FLAG TO SOUND: the B5/B6 boundary moves from 12.5 to 13.0s and the sign-off now starts at 11.5s, so the kettle-tick clearance in SND-D01-007 needs checking again. That call belongs to sound, not the script.

FLAG TO DESIGN AND THE PRODUCER: ART-LOCK-0700 changes. The B1 lock screen now shows 7:00 with one generic notification banner beneath it, its text too small to read, and no app name, icon, date or status-bar text.
FLAG TO THE DIRECTOR: B2's first angle has to show the thumb crossing the glaze at the dripper's foot as the hand closes. How that is framed is the director's call.

The filter is pressed in and the grounds are spooned in off screen, in the B2/B3 cut. If the director wants the filter on screen, it goes into B2's second angle from a stack in front of the mug so the hand never reaches over the phone, and the pace has to be checked again.

With the sign-off, the organic B6 frame holds 8 words ('Shop the Solace dripper. Link in bio.' plus 'Solace'). I treat the sign-off as a brand mark, not card copy. If the 7-word ceiling is read to include it, the organic B6 drops the sign-off, because its card already names Solace.

'7:00' and '7:05' dramatise the key message ('A five-minute ritual...') and are not a brew-time claim. Back after.', which still holds both ends of the window without clock times. The B1 lock screen keeps 7:00, which is just the time of day.

The B4b rings are assumed to come from the phone's vibration passing through the mug, with the fingertip grip. If they don't show on the day, production reinforces the vibration practically. A card or VO must not stand in for them.

Hero-unit fallback (PROP-01): if the hero unit has no glaze pool at the foot, its speck and the thin break at the rim become the mark. The thumb crosses it in B2, and it faces the lens in B5, B6 and D02-2. If the unit shows neither, the whole legible dripper plus the B5 card carries the fact.

evidence.specificity: The director, casting, design and sound teams could each break this down without calling back. Two lines carry the turn and the product: in B4b, "The phone rattles against the wood and the coffee shivers into fine rings. About 1.0s in, the rattle stops, the rings flatten, and her hand stays where it is." In B2, "the thumb passes over the glaze pooled unevenly at its foot without stopping." Sound gets real sources to record, ending on "Room tone; off screen, the kettle ticking as it cools." Casting gets a clear brief: "NORA appears only as hands and forearms." Design gets a lock screen it can build: "7:00 with one generic notification banner beneath it, its text too small to read, and no app name, icon, date or status-bar text." The scope creep from the last round is gone. B2 now says "The card sits clear of the dripper in both angles." The m/s speeds, cm measurements, reading rate and SH shot labels have been removed. Card timings are written into the beats: "The card comes up at 9.5s as the rings flatten, holds to 11.5s."
evidence.distinctiveness: The swap test now fails for a competitor's dripper. The glaze pool the thumb crosses in B2 is the same mark "B5 later turns to the lens," so "Hand-glazed stoneware." names something we watched a hand touch. The turn belongs to this idea alone: a buzz that "gets as far as the rings in her coffee and no further," answered by "Everyone else gets you at 7:05." It stays at 8, not 9, for three reasons. Turning the phone face-down to make coffee is a familiar move in this category. The set texture, "a chipped white mug," is taken word for word from the taste notes' own list of examples. And the new D02-2 headline, "Out from 7:00. Back at 7:05.", can be misread on a bare product plate (see note 2).
evidence.fit:
All six previous notes were addressed:
1. Measurements and working history are removed.
2. The spot is retimed exactly as asked ("B3 4.5-7.0 ... B6 13.0-15.0"). The 7:05 card now waits for the rings to flatten.
3. The product is in the turn: "The Solace dripper stands just past the mug, on the side away from the phone, in frame for the whole beat."
4. The glaze is shown before it is named, via the thumb in B2.
5. D02-2 now carries both clock times on its own: "Out from 7:00. Back at 7:05."
6. B1 is observable: "The hand doesn't slow: it flips the phone in passing," with the notification banner and the flag to ART-LOCK-0700.

The route's idea is recognisable and sharper than written. "Nobody gets you before the pour." / "Everyone else gets you at 7:05." is R1's "Before the phone, the inbox, or anyone else gets a piece of you" said in 12 words of text. Only the three verified facts are stated ("Hand-glazed stoneware."; "made in small batches"; "it still goes in the dishwasher"). Both must-includes are met, with a 3.5s product hold. The one break from the route, cutting the window shot, is named and tied to the taste notes. It stays at 8, not 9, because the D02-2 headline, which also serves as the DTC product image, still needs one small fix.
evidence.craft:
The timing can be performed. The beats run back to back from 0 to 15 with no VO ("0 spoken words in 15s"), four cards of 2 to 6 words, and each card held for 1.5 to 3.0s. Continuity holds from B1 to B6: the phone lands against the mug and "still touches the face-down phone's edge" through B4b, and in B5 and B6 it lies "face-down and dark." Physics is thought through: "A full wrap would add mass and damp the vibration, which would mute the rings." Rights are named and left pending, with scope and owner: "RIGHT, PENDING: a hand-performer release ... Owner: producer ... Not cleared." It stays at 8, not 9, for four reasons:
- The B2 card lands on top of the thumb moment it is meant to leave clear.
- The paid B6 frame shows the brand name twice ("Shop the Solace dripper." over a "Solace" sign-off).
- One cross-reference is wrong: "S2's real detail, the kettle's scorch band" names a detail that S2 doesn't contain.
- Two rights are not listed: the location and the typeface.

notes.target: D01-B2 on_screen_text timing (first angle vs. cut mid-carry)
notes.note: Take the card off the thumb moment. "Nobody gets you before the pour." is up from 1.5s, over the first angle, which is exactly when the thumb crosses the glaze pool. That quiet action is what B5's "Hand-glazed stoneware." pays off. A muted viewer will be reading six words and miss the thumb, so the demonstration you added turns back into an assertion. Keep the first angle (lift and thumb) free of text. Bring the card up on the cut mid-carry and hold it to 4.5s, and write its in-time into the beat, e.g. "card comes up on the cut, about 2.5s, holds to 4.5s." If six words then get less than about 2.0s, shorten the first angle, not the card.
notes.source: Craft brief: "The story must read from picture and on-screen text alone" and "one card per roughly 2 seconds"; craft brief calibration: "demonstrated rather than asserted"; taste notes: "Restraint over explanation."

notes.target: D02-2 headline (and its legal fallback in assumptions)
notes.note: "Out from 7:00. Back at 7:05." has no subject. On a bare product plate, next to "Shop the Solace dripper.", "Out ... Back at ..." reads like a stock notice ("back in stock", a batch drop), especially from a brand whose other still says "made in small batches." A shopper can take it as a restock time. Name the register your decision claims: "Out of office: 7:00-7:05." It keeps both clock times in five words, keeps the dry edge, and points straight at R1's "the inbox." Move the legal fallback into the same register, e.g. "Out of office for the pour."
notes.source: Quality bar, Fit (serves the single-minded proposition); craft brief sound-off rule (each asset reads from its own picture and text); taste notes: "Dry over sentimental"; route R1 central idea: "the inbox."

notes.target: D01-B6 on_screen_text, cta, and the 7-word/sign-off assumption
notes.note: The paid B6 frame reads "Shop the Solace dripper." with "Solace" directly beneath it: the brand name twice in five words. The organic version runs to eight words and depends on a product name that is still unconfirmed. Make the B6 card "Shop the dripper." (organic: "Shop the dripper. Link in bio.") and let the Solace sign-off name the brand. The organic frame then lands at seven words with the sign-off, and you can delete the assumption about whether the ceiling counts it. The end card also stops waiting on the product-name confirmation. The still sublines can keep "Shop the Solace dripper." until the name is confirmed.
notes.source: Craft brief: CTA rule (specific verb + destination) and "at most 7 words per card"; taste notes: "Restraint over explanation."

notes.target: Decisions list: B3 real-detail decision, D02-2 decision, timings decision, B4a/B4b decision
notes.note: Fix one cross-reference and remove the last revision history. "D02-1 carries the pouring hand and S2's real detail, the kettle's scorch band" is wrong, because S2 as written shows only "the gooseneck spout." Reword it to "D02-1 carries the pouring hand and the kettle's scorch band, which B3 leaves out." Then state each decision in the present tense, as the script rather than as a changelog. Cut "The D02-2 headline is now", "I made the still hold", "New timings:" and "The picture now shows what the beat sheet claims." Keep the SND-D01-007 flag to sound exactly as it is.
notes.source: Quality bar, Craft: "every cross-reference to another department's IDs is right"; previous review note 1 (cut negotiation and working history).

(2) The typeface licence for the cards, still copy and the "Solace" sign-off, which is set as type until a lockup is supplied. keep: The B1 hook: the hand "doesn't slow: it flips the phone in passing," with a readable 7:00 and one unreadable notification banner, and no card or VO over it.
The B2 thumb crossing the glaze pooled at the dripper's foot, paid off by the same mark facing the lens in B5, B6 and D02-2, with no card or VO pointing at it.

The B4a/B4b line-up of phone, mug and dripper; the fingertip grip; the coffee shivering into rings and flattening while her hand stays put; and the 7:05 card arriving only as the rings flatten at 9.5s.

characters.role_in_story: Principal and the only person on screen. She appears as hands and forearms only, seen in D01-B1, B2, B4a, B4b and D02-1. B3 shows only the spout. The script sets her name and gender. Habit: every weekday at 7:00 she makes the pour before anyone else gets any of her. Backstory, not a lock: she keeps her lists on paper rather than in the phone, which gives her a writer's callus on the right middle finger. It adds no prop, scene or copy. Playable objective: get the coffee poured and her fingertips on the mug while the phone gets nothing back from her. Age: playing 33-39, target 36. This is a choice, not a story need. It sits inside the 25-40 audience, it is old enough for the habit to look long-standing, and it reads in the creased knuckles. Heritage: not specified. The skin value is the casting choice, and a hand double is matched on the anchors, not on heritage. Defaults broken: the category's default hand is late-20s, pale and slim, with a gloss manicure and stacked gold rings on a linen cuff. The generator's stock hand is long, tapered, poreless and light-skinned. I break both because 'Hands before faces' only works if the hand isn't stock. A stock hand also drifts toward the generic luxury imagery the brief rules out.
characters.screen_presence: One-frame read: a broad, square hand in its mid-thirties, with medium-deep skin, a warm undertone (#6F4A34), creased knuckles and short bare nails. Two raised veins run from the wrist across the back of each hand. They are age texture and are not locked, because heat and hand height change them. The hand flips the buzzing phone face-down in passing, without looking, and is already moving on toward the rack. The hand never searches or hovers: it lands on an object, takes it and lets go. It lifts the dripper out of the rack the way it would lift a mug it uses every day, and the thumb crosses the pooled glaze at the foot without stopping. During the pour the forearm stays still and only the wrist circles. Between actions the hand stops completely: it lies flat and doesn't tap. On the mug, the fingertips touch it without gripping it, and they stay there. Conclusion earned: this hand has done this every morning for years.
characters.performance_style: Understated. Silent: no dialogue, no lip-sync, no VO. No face is cast. At rest the hand lies flat and does nothing. Every move plays at the real pace of a daily habit and is never slowed for the camera (taste note: no slow motion to make something look expensive). The flip and the carry toward the rack are one move, with no pause and no glance down. The pour is a steady, thin spiral, and the stream never wobbles or gets corrected. Her one change is the held hand at B4b. As the phone rattles against the mug, nothing in her hand moves: no flinch, no squeeze, no drift toward the phone. The rings in the coffee are the only movement under her hand, and they come from the phone, never from her grip. The mug stays on the counter. The refusal plays as stillness, not effort.
characters.wardrobe_fit_notes: Height 167 cm (range 165-169). She is the only principal, so there is no one to scale against. Medium build, shoulders level with the hips. The hand is about 18 cm long and 8.5 cm across the knuckles. Right-handed. The mole marks the right hand and the scar marks the left. Whichever hand the director's shot list puts on the product, that hand's mark must read. The director's restage makes the pour left-handed, so she must pour a steady, thin spiral with her left hand (tested at the casting call; see blockers). In D02-1, continuity on the pouring hand rests on the left-hand scar, the build, the skin and the knuckle creases. Product scale: in a one-hand grip on the dripper, glaze must show on both sides of the hand. So the 8.5 cm knuckle breadth must be at least 2 cm less than the dripper dimension the knuckles cross in the director's B2/B4a grip. In a grip over the rim, that is the rim diameter. In a side grip around the body, it is the height. If the dripper has a handle, the knuckles close on the handle instead, and no finger may cross the body on the lens side. If the dimension that applies is under 10.5 cm, casting reopens the hand breadth. The dimensions and the grip are pending (see blockers). Sleeves stop at least 5 cm above the wrist bone on both arms, including with an arm raised to pour, so no cuff crosses the dripper, the kettle, the stream or the mug. The sleeve must differ in value from the skin (#6F4A34) and from the glaze, so the edge of the hand reads against each. Nothing on the fingers or wrists. A ring or watch would click on stoneware over the designed sound, including the phone's tick against the mug, and a watch would add a second clock against 7:00 and 7:05. Joint lock, stylist: nails short, natural and unpolished, filed straight; right thumb cuticle slightly ragged; skin matte, with no lotion sheen; forearm hair sparse, fine and dark (#2A1E17) along the outer edge of both forearms. The stylist decides whether the hair stays or goes, and it is then the same in every setup.
visual_identity_anchors: [macro] Build: a broad, square hand, 8.5 cm across the knuckles against a wrist about 6 cm across. Short, blunt fingers: the middle finger is about 7 cm, shorter than the palm is wide. This breaks the generator's long, tapered hand. Both hands match.

[macro] Skin: medium-deep, warm undertone, #6F4A34 on the back of the hand and the forearm, with visible pores. Palms and fingertip pads: medium, warm undertone, #B3886A. These words go with the hex codes into the hand-double call and every prompt. Reject any take that reads lighter, greyer or olive.
[micro] Knuckle creases on both hands: every knuckle is creased and darker than the skin around it (deep, warm undertone, #4A2F20). This is the locked age marker. The veins are not locked.
[micro] Right hand: a flat 4 mm mole (#3B2519) on the back of the hand, 2 cm toward the wrist from the middle-finger knuckle. The left hand has none. Reject any take with a mole on the left.

[micro] Left hand: a pale, flat, matte scar about 10 mm long (#8A6650, lighter than the skin around it) across the back of the index finger's middle joint. It shows when the hand closes on a handle. The right hand has none. Reject any take with it on the right.

assumptions: NORA is the only character the script names. The beat sheet lists her in S1-S3. S4, D01-B5, D01-B6 and D02-2 have no person in them. No one else is cast or added.
No face is cast, because the script shows NORA as hands and forearms only. If an edit adds her face, casting reopens to set face anchors, so the generator never sets them by default.

NORA is fictional and not modelled on any real person. She is not presented as a customer or an expert, and there is no testimonial. No reference imagery was supplied or inspected. Nothing here clears the rights to make her, whether generated or live (see blockers).

Skin lock: 'medium-deep, warm undertone' goes with #6F4A34 (back of the hand and forearm) and 'medium, warm undertone' with #B3886A (palms and fingertip pads). These phrases apply in the style bible, the hand-double call and every prompt. They are my reading of the hex values, not a measured match. A live hand double is matched by eye under the shoot's key light.

Changes to the anchors this round. The writer's callus is now backstory only, because most grips press it against the index finger, so it cannot hold continuity. The raised veins are now unlocked age texture in screen_presence, because heat and hand height change them. A new permanent mark, the left-hand scar, gives the pouring hand its own anchor, the way the mole marks the right hand.

Two review notes are reconciled here. The film director's note wants the left-handed pour on record, with a left-handed test at the hand-double call. The later note wants the per-shot hand list and the kettle-handle geometry cut from casting. So the left-handed pour appears once, in wardrobe_fit_notes, as something the performer must be able to do, and its test is in the live-performer blocker. Which hand does what in each shot, and where the kettle handle sits, belong to the director's shot list. The 0.9 L gooseneck size comes from the director's note, not from the script. Casting's reading is that a right-handed person pouring with the left hand is plausible as a daily habit, because of where the kettle lives.

Every generated take is checked for the mark on the hand in use: the scar on the left, the mole on the right, never swapped. Generators default to a right-handed pour, so D02-1 is the take most at risk.
The mug stays on the counter through B4b. The script's B5 opens 'moments later' with the mug and hand gone, so no lift is performed on screen.
The market is assumed to be the US, based on the $ price and 'link in bio'. Coffee equipment is not age-restricted, so no code minimum applies.

It is an assumption, not a verified fact, that the dripper comes in one size and has no handle. The hand-scale rule depends on the dripper's dimensions and the director's grip (see blockers). The 2 cm margin, about 1 cm of glaze showing on each side of the hand, is my number.

Glaze separation. The glaze colour isn't specified; the route gives only the palette of terracotta, cream and soft grey. The risky case is terracotta, which sits close to #6F4A34 in both hue and value, so the hand could merge with the dripper at B2, B4a and D02-1. That would be a hand hiding the product through tone rather than size. The skin value stays fixed, because it is a casting choice with stated reasons: it breaks both the category's default hand and the generator's. If the client locks a terracotta glaze, separation at B2, B4a and D02-1 goes to the film director and the cinematographer as a named check (light, sleeve value, background). Owner: film director and cinematographer. Status: pending until the glaze is confirmed. A cream or soft grey glaze separates by value and needs only the sleeve rule.
No human-review flags apply: no child, no disability or visible difference, no religious dress, no pregnancy, and no one aged 70 or over.

blockers.issue: Rights for a generated NORA are not cleared.
blockers.resolution: Source: the chosen generator's output-use terms, plus any AI-content labelling the platforms require for paid and organic social. Scope: D01 (15 s, 9:16) and D02-1 (4:5), on social and the DTC site, in the US. Owner: producer. Status: pending.

blockers.issue: A live hand performer, if one is used for any insert or for the D02-1 still, needs a release, a match to the anchors and a tested left-handed pour.
blockers.resolution: Source: a hand-model release. Scope: D01 and D02-1, on social and the DTC site, in the US, for a term the producer sets to match the media plan. The performer must be 21 or older and match all five anchors. Skin is called in words: 'medium-deep, warm undertone' (#6F4A34, back of the hand) and 'medium, warm undertone' (#B3886A, palms), matched by eye under the shoot's key light. The right-hand mole and the left-hand scar may be applied by makeup (joint lock, stylist). Tested at the casting call: (1) with the left hand, pour a steady, thin spiral from a 0.9 L gooseneck, filled as for the shoot, onto grounds in a dripper, with no wobble or correction in the stream; (2) hold the right fingertips still on a mug through a 3 s take while a phone buzzes against it. Owner: producer. Status: pending.

blockers.issue: The client has not supplied the dripper's height, rim diameter, body diameter at the foot, whether it has a handle, the sizes sold or the glaze colour. The director has not yet named the B2/B4a grip. The hand-scale rule and the skin-to-glaze separation both depend on these.
blockers.responsible_agent: producer (request to the client, Solace Home Goods); film_director (grip call)
blockers.resolution: The client confirms the height, the rim diameter, the body diameter at the foot, whether there is a handle, the sizes sold and the glaze colour. The director names the B2/B4a grip: over the rim, a side grip around the body, or on the handle. The threshold is then set against the dimension that grip lays the knuckles across. If it is under 10.5 cm, casting reopens the hand breadth before generation or a live casting call. If the glaze is terracotta, separation at B2, B4a and D02-1 goes to the film director and the cinematographer as a named check, and the skin value does not change. Owner: producer (client request) and film director (grip). Status: pending.

evidence.specificity: The stylist, director and cinematographer can each act on the bible without asking a question. The hand is fixed in numbers: "The hand is about 18 cm long and 8.5 cm across the knuckles." The new mark is fully specified: "[micro] Left hand: a pale, flat, matte scar about 10 mm long (#8A6650, lighter than the skin around it) across the back of the index finger's middle joint... Reject any take with it on the right." The stylist gets a constraint rather than a costume: "Sleeves stop at least 5 cm above the wrist bone on both arms, including with an arm raised to pour." Previous notes 1 and 2 are fully addressed. The callus is now backstory only ("Backstory, not a lock"). The veins are moved to screen_presence ("They are age texture and are not locked"). That leaves five permanent anchors: build, skin, knuckle creases, the right-hand mole and the left-hand scar. Build and skin are tagged macro.
evidence.distinctiveness: The behaviour and constraints only work inside R1's 7:00-to-7:05 idea. The jewellery ban is argued from this film: "A ring or watch would click on stoneware over the designed sound, including the phone's tick against the mug, and a watch would add a second clock against 7:00 and 7:05." The turn is cast as physics, not emotion: "The rings in the coffee are the only movement under her hand, and they come from the phone, never from her grip." The skin-to-glaze risk is tied to the route's own palette ("The risky case is terracotta, which sits close to #6F4A34 in both hue and value"). It stays at 8, not 9, because the locked marks (a mole and a scar) are sound continuity devices that would fit on any hand. The idea-specific texture lives in behaviour and in the unlocked backstory.
evidence.fit: The bible delivers the script's hands-only decision and the taste note, and it argues why the hand itself must be cast: "I break both because 'Hands before faces' only works if the hand isn't stock. A stock hand also drifts toward the generic luxury imagery the brief rules out." The category default is named and broken ("late-20s, pale and slim, with a gloss manicure and stacked gold rings on a linen cuff"). The must-include product role is protected at the level of the body, through the grip-dependent scale rule and the reopen clause. The rules on fictional talent and testimonials are met: "She is not presented as a customer or an expert, and there is no testimonial." No product claim is made. The playable objective carries R1: "get the coffee poured and her fingertips on the mug while the phone gets nothing back from her."
evidence.craft: All five previous notes are fixed. Per-shot hand assignment and kettle-handle geometry are gone, replaced by: "Whichever hand the director's shot list puts on the product, that hand's mark must read." role_in_story now reads "seen in D01-B1, B2, B4a, B4b and D02-1. B3 shows only the spout." The scale rule now follows the grip: "In a grip over the rim, that is the rim diameter. In a side grip around the body, it is the height... If the dimension that applies is under 10.5 cm, casting reopens the hand breadth." The glaze check has an owner and a status: "the skin value does not change... Owner: film director and cinematographer. Status: pending until the glaze is confirmed." Every right is left pending with its source, scope and owner. What holds it at 8 rather than 9: the assumptions still read as a revision log ("Changes to the anchors this round...", "Two review notes are reconciled here..."). There is also a small overlap between the left-hand scar and the knuckle-crease lock, and blocker 3 asks for a foot diameter that the scale rule never uses. A senior casting director would clean these up before sending, but none of them blocks the bible.

notes.target: assumptions: 'Changes to the anchors this round...' and 'Two review notes are reconciled here...'
notes.note: Rewrite these two entries as the current decisions and drop the history. For example: 'The writer's callus is backstory only; the veins are unlocked age texture; the left-handed pour is a performer requirement from the director's restage and is tested in blocker 2.' Cut 'Casting's reading is that a right-handed person pouring with the left hand is plausible as a daily habit, because of where the kettle lives.' Where the kettle sits is the director's set logic, and the blocker already sets the test. The bible should read as the current lock, not as a record of the review rounds.
notes.source: Quality bar, specificity: 'can the next department act on it without asking a question?'; 'Detail that does a later department's job... costs craft'; craft brief: 'Leave holds, framing and the product hand per shot to the director'

notes.target: visual_identity_anchors: '[micro] Knuckle creases on both hands: every knuckle is creased and darker...' vs '[micro] Left hand: a pale... scar... across the back of the index finger's middle joint'
notes.note: The two locks cover the same joint. Add one clause to the scar anchor so the generator doesn't pick one and drop the other: 'On this joint the pale scar crosses the dark crease and breaks it; the crease shows on either side of the scar.' Add the same wording to the hand-double makeup instruction in blocker 2, so an applied scar sits the same way.
notes.source: Craft brief: 'Anchors are what continuity locks'; 'Generators drift young, symmetrical, poreless'

notes.target: wardrobe_fit_notes: product-scale rule; blocker 3
notes.note: Blocker 3 asks the client for 'the body diameter at the foot', but the scale rule never uses it. The script's B2 lift has the thumb crossing the glaze pooled at the foot, so a low grip is a real option for the director. Add a third case in one sentence: 'In a low grip at the foot, the dimension is the body diameter at the foot.' Keep the same 2 cm margin and the same reopen consequence. This keeps the check on hand breadth only, and leaves framing out of it.
notes.source: Creative director's reject: 'hands that hide the product'; script D01-B2: 'the thumb passes over the glaze pooled unevenly at its foot'; brief must-include: 'A clear product role in the story'

notes.target: role_in_story: 'Backstory, not a lock: ... a writer's callus on the right middle finger.'
notes.note: Add 'never prompted, never applied by makeup'. A prompt writer who copies role_in_story could otherwise put an unlocked callus on some takes and not others, which is the continuity break the anchor change was meant to remove.
notes.source: Craft brief calibration: 'recorded, not prompted'; 'Anchors are what continuity locks'

keep: The one-frame read and its earned conclusion: 'a broad, square hand in its mid-thirties... creased knuckles and short bare nails... Conclusion earned: this hand has done this every morning for years.'
The named category default and generator stock hand, each broken with a reason tied to 'Hands before faces' and the must-avoid on generic luxury.
The playable objective: 'get the coffee poured and her fingertips on the mug while the phone gets nothing back from her.'
The B4b performance: 'no flinch, no squeeze, no drift toward the phone... The refusal plays as stillness, not effort.'
The five permanent anchors, with build and skin tagged macro, and the reject-if-swapped rules for the right-hand mole and left-hand scar.
Skin locked in words plus hex, #6F4A34 for the back of the hand and #B3886A for the palms, with 'Reject any take that reads lighter, greyer or olive.'
The grip-dependent scale rule with its 10.5 cm reopen threshold.
The ring and watch ban, argued from the sound design and the 7:00/7:05 clock.
The terracotta separation check: skin value fixed, owner film director and cinematographer, status pending.
The no-face clause with 'casting reopens to set face anchors, so the generator never sets them by default.'
All three blockers, each with source, scope, owner and pending status; the hand-double tests for the left-handed pour and the still fingertips.

locations.description:
LOC-01 · INT. NORA'S KITCHEN - COUNTER. One set carries all four script headings: S1 (D01-B1 flip; D01-B2 lift and seat), S2 (D01-B3 pour and bloom; D02-1), S3 (D01-B4a set-down; D01-B4b second buzz) and S4 (D01-B5 to D01-B6 hold; D02-2). It is a studio build. spatial_layout lists what gets built and what exists only in the story.
Place and year: USA, 2026, a pre-war rental (ASSUMED from the USD price and 'link in bio'). That means a 12-hour lock screen, a USB-C phone, a gas range and NEMA 5-15 at OUT-01, which sits below the top and in no frame. No window view, signage, street or plates appear.
History: NORA has cooked for one here for about four years (ASSUMED). The phone charged on this counter overnight, not by her bed (PROP-08). The dripper lives dry in the rack between mornings (PROP-04 ST1), and the filters live in the upper cabinet. This morning, before D01-B1, she put the kettle on RANGE-01 and set the chipped mug on its spot (PROP-03 ST1).
One real detail per scene (taste notes):
- S1: the tide line inside the empty mug, 2 cm below the rim, the level she fills to every day (PROP-03 ST1).
- S2: the kettle's gas-scorch band. It is seen in D02-1 only, because the script drops it from D01-B3 on purpose.
- S3: the coffee rings bending TILE-01's reflected edge, with the phone against the mug (the script's own detail).
- S4: the phone left face-down where she flipped it, its mug-side edge now meeting bare oak where the mug stood. Mark 2 is texture only. D02-2 stays bare on purpose as the DTC image.
The rack, mug and cable are texture ('Real kitchens have a dish rack and a charging cable'). The window is never in frame, and nobody looks out of it.
Blank surfaces (generators add logos here): dripper exterior, phone case and back, phone glass except the lock screen, kettle, mug, plate, tumbler, rack and tray, filters, cable, adapter, grommet ring, cabinet fronts, and TILE-01 (no pattern, decal or maker mark).
Only text: the D01-B1 lock screen, composited, top toward 90°. It shows '7:00' in #1B1F24 generic sans on a flat #E4E7EA field (13:1). Below that is one generic banner: a rounded #FFFFFF bar holding a blank #B8BDC3 icon square and two #8A9097 lines too small to read, with no glyphs. There is no date or status bar.
Motion: hands, water, steam (D01-B3 to D01-B4b), coffee rings (D01-B4b) and phone light (D01-B1, D01-B4b). Nothing moves in D01-B5 to D01-B6 or in D02-2.
Fallback: the dressing is flop-safe (no legible set text, a centred lens cut-out), and the lock screen is composited after any flop.
Frame locks list the props besides the product, 5 at most. PROP-07 is the surface in every frame and is not counted.
- D01-B1: 02/03/08.
- D01-B2: 02/03/04/08.
- D01-B3: 02 (its face-down wall-D end)/03/05/06. PROP-08 is plugged in, off frame.
- D01-B4a: 02/03/05 (ST5, spent filter in the cone)/08.
- D01-B4b: 02/03/05 (ST5)/08.
- D01-B5 to D01-B6: 02 only. PROP-08 is plugged in, off frame.
- D02-1: 02/03/05/06, with PROP-08 struck.
- D02-2: none.
No canister, spoon, filter stack or filter box is in any frame. The filter and grounds go in during the D01-B2/D01-B3 cut, as the script decides.
Palette shares are of the D01-B4a counter view. The 8% outside the palette is NORA's hand and sleeve (cast and wardrobe) and coffee #3B2416. Per-frame note for D01-B3 and D02-1: PROP-06 #A4583F terracotta matte enamel is the accent at about 12% of frame (0% of the master). The set breaks no taste note; the D01-B3 break is the script's.
locations.spatial_layout:
Studio BUILD for a small crew (ASSUMED).
Story room: 2.6 W × 3.4 D × 2.75 H m. Walls run clockwise in plan: A entrance (y 0), B (x 0), C window (y 340), D counter (x 260). The origin is corner A/B; x runs along A toward D and y toward C, in cm, and heights are from the floor. Bearings: 0° = toward wall C, clockwise, so 90° faces the wall-D backsplash and 270° faces wall B. With the run on wall D, the rack lies at frame right of the mug as seen from the aisle, so the D01-B2 carry runs right to left as D01-B1 and D01-B2 say.
Openings:
- DOOR-01, wall A, x 110-192: one 82 cm leaf hinged at x 192, swinging out into the hall. The view through it is the unlit hall, which is in no frame.
- WIN-01, wall C, x 160-250, sill 100 cm, head 215 cm. No sash, glass or translight. A diffusion frame fills the opening as the key's position (the unit and the diffusion are the DP's), so nothing beyond it can be seen.
Plan (story):
- Wall D, starting from wall A: a base cabinet at y 0-40. Then RANGE-01, a 76 cm four-burner gas range at x 196-260, y 40-116, with a hood above. The kettle heats on its front burner at 212/97, which causes the scorch band, and ticks there off frame in D01-B5 to D01-B6, about 1.8 m toward wall A from the dripper. Then the counter run at y 116-340, with the sink at y 125-185 and FAUCET-01, a single-lever gooseneck at 254/155 (the knock that chipped the mug).
- FRIDGE-01, 61 × 70 cm, in corner B/C at x 0-61, y 270-340, front facing 180°.
- The aisle, x 70-196, stays clear to 2.1 m.
BUILT:
(1) PROP-07 counter run on wall D: y 116-340, x 197-260, top at 91 cm, on plain base cabinets with blank slab fronts. The sink cut-out is at x 204-250, y 125-185, dry and empty (no dish, sponge, soap or brush), with Mark 3 at its front corner.
(2) Wall-D backsplash flat: y 116-340, floor to 275 cm. Upper cabinets at y 116-200 only, x 227-260, 145-230 cm, with a soffit to the ceiling. Nothing hangs over the work zone.
(3) TILE-01 on wall D: one course of 7.5 × 15 cm matte #D5D8D2 tile laid horizontally at y 250-340, bottom edge at 112.0 cm, top edge at 119.5 cm, with #C4C6C0 grout and a bullnose end at y 250. It is left from an older splash whose lower courses were skimmed and painted (ASSUMED). It stays empty: nothing leans on it or hangs from it, so it adds no lock.
(4) Bare #6B6E67 flats, floor to 275 cm, for the gloss mirror paths: wall B (x 0, y 0-340); wall A (y 0, x 0-260, solid, because DOOR-01 is story only); and wall C (y 340, x 0-260, with the WIN-01 opening). Walls A and B are wild for access and close for the hero setups.
(5) CEIL-01: a flat matte #E6E2DA ceiling at 275 cm over x 0-260, y 0-340. The DP may cut lamp openings; the prelight confirms that no gloss surface sees one.
NOT BUILT (story only, in no frame): RANGE-01 and its hood, FRIDGE-01, FAUCET-01, DOOR-01 and the base cabinet at y 0-40. Any frame that shows y < 185 needs FAUCET-01 built. The kettle is heated off-set. The WIN-01 translight is struck.
OUT-01: a NEMA 5-15 duplex with an ivory plate, on the wall-D flat inside the base cabinet at y 322, 30 cm above the floor. It is below the top and in no frame. PROP-08 reaches it through a Ø 2.0 cm hole in the top's back strip, centred at 258/322 and lined with a flush black grommet #2A2C2E. Nothing runs on wall D above the top.
Card area: the wall-D paint from 125 cm up, at y 240-340, stays bare for composited cards. TILE-01 stops 5.5 cm below it.
Coffee mirror line (D01-B4b): the coffee surface is at 98.5 cm at 232.7/295, and wall D is 27.3 cm behind it along x. A lens at height h and horizontal distance d from the mug sees wall D in the coffee at 98.5 + (h − 98.5) × 27.3/d cm. TILE-01's 112.0 cm edge lands mid-coffee at h = 98.5 + 0.494·d: 118.3 cm at d 40, 123.2 at d 50, 128.2 at d 60. The 119.5 cm edge needs h = 98.5 + 0.769·d. Off the x axis, replace 27.3 with 27.3/sin(bearing of the lens-to-mug line). The mirror point on wall D then sits at y = 295 + 27.3/tan(bearing), which is inside TILE-01's y 250-340 for bearings of 31-149°. Lens placement is the DP's.
TILE-01 and the dripper: the rim tops out at 99.5 cm. For any lens at or above 99.5 cm, the dripper's outline is backed by oak or by paint below 99.5 cm and never by TILE-01, a margin of 12.5 cm. A lower hero angle needs a re-check.
Marks (centre x/y). Every mark is hard, and this is the one set for every department.
- PROP-07: 15 oak strips of 4.2 cm running along y, with seams at x = 260 − 4.2n.
- PROP-04 rack: x 220-252, y 190-236. PROP-01 stands in it at 232.7/213.
- PROP-03 mug and PROP-01 ST2-ST3: 232.7/295, 45 cm from wall C.
- PROP-01 ST4-ST5: 232.7/280, 60 cm from wall C, on clean oak. The D01-B4a set-down lands within ±1 cm, and props reset it exactly for D01-B5.
- Carries run along the x 232.7 strip centre: 82 cm in D01-B2 and 15 cm in D01-B4a.
- PROP-02 phone: long axis along x, top toward 90°, port at the aisle end. ST1 is face-up at 230.0/304.8, port at 222.3/304.8. ST2-ST4 is face-down at 230.0/302.8 (case x 222.3-237.7, y 299.0-306.6), its mug-side edge touching the mug at 232.7/299, port at 222.3/302.8.
- PROP-08 route: from the port, out along the phone's axis to x 218. Then along x 218 toward wall C through its loop (x 210-218, y 308-318 in ST1; x 211-218, y 308-316 in ST2) to y 322. Then along y 322 to x 258, and down the grommet to OUT-01. It never enters y < 302 and never runs up wall D.
- PROP-07 Mark 2 (texture): front edge, x 197-201, y 250-330.
The foot (x 227.7-237.7) straddles the seams at 230.6 and 234.8, each 2.1 cm off centre. Clear zone (D01-B5 to D01-B6, D02-2): x 221.7-243.7, y 269-291, 0-25 cm above the top. The phone lies 8 cm beyond it.
palette: #533C2B white-oak butcher block finished with a tobacco-brown tinted hardwax oil, matte (PROP-07 top; the builder matches a sample board to this hex under the 18% card), with #3B2B1F hairline glue seams. Dominant, 45% of the master (D01-B4a counter view). Untinted oiled white oak ambers to about #B08A5E and would drop the product body to 2.3:1. The earlier #7A5A3E left the glaze pool at 2.3:1 and the raw flange at 1.9:1.
#6B6E67 grey-green landlord paint: washable eggshell on every flat and the backsplash, semi-gloss on the upper cabinets and base fronts. Secondary, 27%.

#F2EFE8 white gloss glaze (PROP-03 mug, PROP-04 plate), with #F1EEE6 bleached crepe paper (PROP-05 collar) and #D5D8D2 pale sage-grey matte tile (TILE-01, the one course on wall D). Neutral, 9%. The #E6E2DA flat ceiling (CEIL-01) is mirror path only, 0% of any frame.

#E3D9C6 oatmeal-cream satin glaze with #5A4636 iron speck, pooling to #B59A72 gloss, with a #C9A77E gloss rim band and a raw #A88663 matte foot. PROP-01 only. Accent, 7%. No other object on the set may carry this cream; TILE-01 is a cool sage-grey.
#77756F stone-grey matte silicone, the PROP-02 bumper (2.2:1 on the oak). Neutral, 3%.
#2A2C2E black matte TPE, the PROP-08 cable jacket and the grommet ring (1.4:1 on the oak). Neutral, 1%.

props.description:
Solace pour-over dripper, the product. Shape and size are ASSUMED from ceramic size-02 cones; no dimensions, colour or finish were supplied.
Form: a handle-less cone, 8.5 cm tall, rim Ø 11.5 cm, 7.5 cm deep to a single 6 mm exit hole 5 mm above the underside. The outer wall is about 18° off vertical, Ø 6.5 cm where it meets the flange. Base flange: outer Ø 10.0 cm, central opening Ø 4.5 cm, outer edge 4 mm tall, top at 0.6 cm.
Material: hand-glazed stoneware (verified).
Glaze: the body is oatmeal-cream satin #E3D9C6 with #5A4636 iron speck (0.5-1.5 mm, about 15 per 10 cm²). Over the rim it breaks thin to a 2 mm gloss band #C9A77E. At the foot it pools unevenly to gloss #B59A72, 3-12 mm tall, filling the fillet between the cone wall and the flange top. The thickest 4 cm arc of that pool is the 'front': the mark her thumb crosses in D01-B2 and the only swap-test detail.
Raw foot (ASSUMED): the flange edge and a 0.8 cm underside band (Ø 10.0 outer, 8.4 inner) are unglazed #A88663 matte. The band stands 1.5 mm proud, so only the band touches a flat counter. On the Ø 8.0 mug the band hangs 2 mm outside the rim and centres the dripper, glazed underside on glazed rim (the D01-B2 click).
Markings: no exterior logo or text. Any maker's stamp goes on the underside, which no frame sees.
Appears in no other location.
props.persistent_state_notes:
The front faces 235° in every state; it is never turned in the hand.
ST1 (D01-B2 first angle, until the lift; the D01-B1 hand exits toward it): upright in PROP-04 at 232.7/213, dry.
ST2 (D01-B2, not before D01-B2): lifted, with the thumb passing over the front glaze pool without stopping. It is carried 82 cm along x 232.7 and seated empty on PROP-03 at 232.7/295, the raw band hanging 2 mm outside the rim. D01-B2 ends on it empty (script).
ST3 (D01-B3; D02-1): same spot. The filter and grounds went in during the D01-B2/D01-B3 cut (PROP-05 ST2 to ST4).
ST4 (D01-B4a to D01-B4b, not before D01-B3): lifted, and the last drip falls from its tip into the coffee. Props drain the cone before the take, so nothing else drips. It is carried 15 cm along x 232.7 and set down at 232.7/280 within ±1 cm, on clean oak, with the spent filter (PROP-05 ST5) still in the cone. D01-B4b holds wherever the take lands.
ST5 (D01-B5 to D01-B6, not before D01-B4b): props reset it exactly on 232.7/280 across the script's 'moments later' cut, with the foot straddling the seams at 230.6 and 234.8 symmetrically. The filter is out and it is empty. The outer glaze is dry, with no coffee, fingerprints or crumbs.
D02-2: ST5, with the mug, phone and cable struck.

props.description:
NORA's phone: a generic 2026 slab, 15 × 7.2 × 0.9 cm.
Case: a stone-grey matte silicone bumper #77756F (15.4 × 7.6 × 1.1 cm) with a blank back plate and one centred rectangular lens cut-out at the top showing two black lenses. It is mirror-symmetric and flop-safe, with no logo and no raised multi-lens module.
Face side: only four corner pads stand about 1.5 mm proud of the glass, and the bumper is open along all four edges between them. Face-down, the case touches the wood and the glass doesn't: the glass rides 1.5 mm off the oak, which gives the D01-B4b glow a path.
USB-C port at the bottom. Its only screen state is the lock screen given in the LOC-01 text spec.
The case reads 2.2:1 on the oak, so the S4 phone reads while staying below the product body's 7.3:1. Charcoal would read 1.0:1 on the deepened oak and vanish.
Appears in no other location.
props.persistent_state_notes:
ST1 (D01-B1, to about 0.8 s): face-up at 230.0/304.8, top toward 90°, plugged in at 222.3/304.8, its mug-side edge 2 cm from the mug. The lock screen lights ('7:00' and the banner, composited) and it buzzes.
ST2 (from about 0.8 s of D01-B1, not before D01-B1; D01-B2 to D01-B4a; D02-1): flipped over its long axis, so the port stays on the axis and the cable stays in. It is set down 2 cm toward the mug, face-down and dark at 230.0/302.8, its mug-side edge touching the mug at 232.7/299. Port at 222.3/302.8. In D01-B3 only its wall-D end is locked. In D02-1 it is unplugged.
ST3 (D01-B4b, about 8.5-9.5 s): same position. The screen lights face-down, so nothing is legible. Light leaks through the open edges onto the oak, 5-15 mm (ASSUMED until the glow test; a secondary cue only). It rattles 3 mm at most, ticking against the mug on its corner pad, then settles back touching the mug. The light is gone when the rattle stops, at about 9.5 s.
ST4 (D01-B5 to D01-B6, not before D01-B4b): face-down and dark at 230.0/302.8, unmoved since the flip. Its mug-side edge now meets bare oak where the mug stood (the S4 detail), 8 cm outside the clear zone.
D02-2: struck.

props.description:
NORA's chipped white mug: a straight-sided diner mug, Ø 8.0 × 9.5 cm, about 330 ml, white gloss #F2EFE8 over a buff body, with no print.
Chip: on the rim at bearing 195°, 7 × 4 mm and 2 mm deep, raw buff #CDBBA0 matte against the gloss, from a knock on FAUCET-01 while rinsing.
Tide line: inside, 2 cm below the rim, #B79C7A. It is the level she fills to every day, and it is the S1 detail, visible inside the empty mug in D01-B1.
The handle points 90°, toward the backsplash, because the phone rests against the mug at 0°.
Appears in no other location.
props.persistent_state_notes:
ST1 (D01-B1 to the start of D01-B2): empty at 232.7/295, handle at 90°, chip at 195°, tide line visible. The phone lands against it at 0°, not before D01-B1.
ST2 (D01-B2, not before D01-B2): PROP-01 seated on it, empty.
ST3 (D01-B3; D02-1): coffee #3B2416 rising, light steam, the phone still touching.

props.description:
Dish rack, used as open storage for the few things she uses daily. Matte white epoxy-coated steel wire #D6D4CD, 46 × 32 × 13 cm, on a grey polypropylene drip tray #BFC0BA, with no maker tag.

Not in it: a cutlery cup, fork, sponge, soap, brush, suds, droplets or standing water. It reads as the place the dripper lives, not a wash-up.
Appears in no other location.
props.persistent_state_notes:
